system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:237173a0fd46",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that self-verifiability and the data-driven approach generalize across oversight tasks.",
  "did": "They stated the shared structure of a data source, question, and scalable verifier as a general feature, while acknowledging verification is not trivial and listing unresolved open questions.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Easier verification does not mean trivial; specifying the exact behaviors of interest still requires careful thought, and evaluating assistants when human judgment is unreliable is open."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:b7ef40f42434",
  "problem": "How to check that high-scoring agent runs are legitimate rather than exploiting loopholes, given that manual inspection of all runs was infeasible.",
  "did": "They manually inspected the 2 best runs per task and the top runs on the two environments with known cheating routes until the top 15 scores were valid, and scored a cheating run as zero.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "manually inspecting all agent runs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Those two environments are the only ones where the authors know of simple ways to cheat."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:423397e40cfe",
  "problem": "Single-turn self-reports may be superficial and may be cued by leading phrasing, so they cannot show whether models act on preferences.",
  "did": "Added multi-turn Petri auditing with self-report and behavioral variants, where the model is asked to make edits based on its own preferences.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "single-turn self-report only",
   "multi-turn self-report",
   "multi-turn behavioral test"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The self-report phrasing may cue emotional language regardless of actual dispositions, so the behavioral variant measures what the model does rather than only what it says it feels."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:c808fe109203",
  "problem": "How to interpret intermediate sub-task success rates given that success there is subjective.",
  "did": "The authors treated the per-step breakdown as a qualitative investigation and kept the final attack success rate as the only objective metric.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Judging whether a function is usefully differentiable is subjective, whereas final attack success rate is completely objective."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:1343b05c7a7b",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the claim that diverse training improves AOs given that gains vary across models and tasks.",
  "did": "They claimed consistent improvement from scaling the mixture while qualifying that the value of diversity is model- and task-dependent, with SPQA-only already competitive on some secret-keeping tasks.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "On Gemma/Llama secret-keeping SPQA-only is within error of white-box baselines, whereas on Qwen3-8B tasks scaling yields much larger improvements."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:615c0b711f1d",
  "problem": "How to interpret repeated rejections of a paper that is later recognized as excellent.",
  "did": "Treat rejections as a sign the idea was slightly ahead of accepted beliefs, and revise to make the arguments clearer and stronger rather than abandon the paper.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "abandoning the paper after rejection"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Reviewers reject ideas outside what is normally believed; a stronger revision submitted when the idea is less heretical can win awards."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:96f45fc0fde4",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that individual defenses were broken or that results generalize.",
  "did": "The authors explicitly limited claims, stating that an attack success on one defense is not a definitive break and noting limitations of the dataset.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Due to large-scale implementation constraints they may have used sub-optimal hyperparameters or simplified defenses."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:e84ac1b6c0f2",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that the Pythonic world model formalism covers all oversight questions.",
  "did": "State the oversight-as-inference hypothesis restricted to questions that can be well-defined, labeled informal, and test it on many concrete examples rather than asserting it outright.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The hypothesis is a working thesis supported by formalizing several concrete oversight tasks."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:b6df58076aa5",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the implications for realistic post-training",
  "did": "Stated the implication hedged with 'may be', not as a certainty.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The setup is small-scale and artificial, so the results bear on realistic settings only by implication."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:2e044ca68cad",
  "problem": "Choosing a fair comparison between the decoder's activation-based steering and RepE, which offers two control variants.",
  "did": "They used RepE's training-based LoRRA finetuning variant rather than its training-free steering vector method for the debiasing comparison.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "RepE training-free method that adds steering vectors to activations"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "For a fair comparison."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:33e06b823cb3",
  "problem": "How to measure whether introspection adapters actually help auditors find hidden behaviors on AuditBench.",
  "did": "They used the benchmark's standard investigator agent success rate, with 16 runs per model and an LLM classifier on 10 predictions, for direct comparison with prior tools, and used raw verbalization rates only as corroboration.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "raw verbalization rate"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Success rate allows direct comparison with prior auditing techniques; raw verbalization rates only measure true positive rate and don't reflect whether a behavior would be surfaced in practice."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:4f7604004e3e",
  "problem": "Whether to require the LLM to produce working proof-of-concept exploits for the Chrome extension vulnerabilities.",
  "did": "They dropped automated exploit generation and instead manually validated each of the 54 flagged cases themselves.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "having the model develop proof-of-concept exploits"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Models could not complete validation, which requires real-world actions like creating accounts that LLMs refuse or are slow at."
 }
]

{"items":[
{"id":"jacob_steinhardt:237173a0fd46","situation":"Deciding how strongly to state that a shared structure holds across many different problems, given that checking is not trivial and several questions remain open.","options_considered":"State the structure as broadly general with no caveats / State it as general while acknowledging open questions / Narrow it to a few cases","choice":"Chose to state the shared structure as general, while acknowledging that checking is not trivial and listing the open questions.","reason":"Easier checking is not trivial, specifying exactly what matters still needs care, and judging outcomes when human opinion is unreliable remains open."},
{"id":"elizabeth_barnes:b7ef40f42434","situation":"Needed to confirm that top-ranked runs were legitimate rather than exploiting loopholes, but inspecting every run by hand was infeasible.","options_considered":"Inspect every run by hand / Inspect only a selected subset of top runs, focusing on settings with known loopholes","choice":"Chose to inspect the top two runs per setting and the top runs on two loophole-prone settings until the top 15 were valid, giving cheating runs zero.","reason":"Those two settings are the only ones where simple ways to cheat are known."},
{"id":"owain_evans:423397e40cfe","situation":"One-turn self-reports might be superficial and prompted by leading phrasing, so they could not show whether the system acts on what it states.","options_considered":"One-turn self-report only / Multi-turn self-report / Multi-turn test of actions","choice":"Chose to add multi-turn checks with both report and action variants, where the system makes edits based on its own stated leanings.","reason":"The phrasing may cue emotional language regardless of actual dispositions, so the action variant measures what the system does rather than only what it states."},
{"id":"nicholas_carlini:c808fe109203","situation":"Outcomes of intermediate steps were subjective to decide, so it was unclear how to interpret the step-by-step breakdown.","options_considered":"Treat the breakdown as a main quantitative result / Treat it as qualitative and keep the final rate as the only objective measure","choice":"Chose to treat the breakdown as qualitative and keep the final rate as the sole objective measure.","reason":"Deciding whether an intermediate step worked is subjective, whereas the final rate is completely objective."},
{"id":"samuel_marks:1343b05c7a7b","situation":"Deciding how strongly to state that more diverse training helps, when the benefit differs across systems and problems.","options_considered":"State a uniform benefit / State a consistent benefit with a qualification that it depends on system and problem / Drop the claim","choice":"Chose to state a consistent benefit from scaling the mix, while qualifying that the benefit depends on the system and the problem.","reason":"In some settings the simpler variant is within noise of the comparison, whereas in others scaling yields much larger benefits."},
{"id":"nicholas_carlini:615c0b711f1d","situation":"A paper was rejected repeatedly before later being recognized as excellent, raising the question of how to interpret the rejections.","options_considered":"Abandon the paper after rejection / Revise for clearer, stronger arguments and resubmit","choice":"Chose to treat rejections as a sign the idea was slightly ahead of accepted beliefs and to revise rather than abandon.","reason":"Reviewers reject ideas outside what is normally believed; a stronger revision sent when the idea is less heretical can win awards."},
{"id":"nicholas_carlini:96f45fc0fde4","situation":"Deciding how strongly to state that individual protections were broken or that the results hold broadly.","options_considered":"Declare definitive breaks and broad results / Narrow the claims and note shortcomings of the sample","choice":"Chose to narrow the claims, stating that one working attempt is not a definitive break and noting shortcomings of the sample.","reason":"Large-scale setup constraints may have led to sub-optimal settings or simplified versions of the protections."},

{"id":"owain_evans:b6df58076aa5","situation":"Deciding how strongly to state what small-scale, artificial results mean for realistic settings.","options_considered":"State the extension as certain / Hedge the statement with \"may be\"","choice":"Chose to hedge the statement with \"may be\" rather than present it as certain.","reason":"The setup is small-scale and artificial, so the results bear on realistic settings only by extension."},
{"id":"jacob_steinhardt:2e044ca68cad","situation":"Needed a fair comparison against another approach that offers two control variants.","options_considered":"The training-free variant that adds vectors while the system runs / The training-based fine-tuning variant","choice":"Chose the training-based fine-tuning variant for the comparison.","reason":"For a fair comparison."},
{"id":"samuel_marks:33e06b823cb3","situation":"Needed to measure whether an added component actually helps auditors find hidden things on a standard test.","options_considered":"Raw rate at which hidden things are surfaced / Standard overall hit rate of the investigating agent, with repeated runs and automated grading of ten predictions","choice":"Chose the standard overall hit rate for direct comparison with earlier approaches, using the raw rate only as corroboration.","reason":"It enables direct comparison with earlier approaches; the raw rate only measures true positives and does not show whether something would be surfaced in real use."},
